content: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) is a chemical compound with the molecular formula HF. It is widely utilized in the petrochemical industry and serves as a component in the production of various superacids. Unlike other hydrogen halides, HF has a boiling point just below room temperature, whereas the others condense at significantly lower temperatures. Aqueous solutions of HF, known as hydrofluoric acid, are highly corrosive. In its solid state, HF forms orthorhombic crystals composed of zig-zag chains of HF molecules. The distance between adjacent molecules in these chains is approximately 2.55 Å. In its liquid state, HF also consists of molecular chains, but these chains are shorter, typically containing only five or six molecules on average. The relatively high boiling point of HF compared to other hydrogen halides, such as HCl, is attributed to the presence of hydrogen bonding between HF molecules. This hydrogen bonding is evident from the persistence of molecular chains even in the liquid phase. Dilute solutions of hydrogen fluoride exhibit weak acidity due to the extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding, which prevents the molecules from readily ionizing into H⁺ and F⁻ ions. Instead, the molecules tend to remain in chains. However, in more concentrated HF solutions, F⁻ ions form soluble complexes with HF molecules, leading to the ionization of remaining HF molecules to compensate for the loss of F⁻ ions. This results in the generation of more H⁺ ions, making concentrated HF an effectively strong acid. Anhydrous hydrogen fluoride is an extremely strong acid, with an acidity comparable to anhydrous sulfuric acid. Hydrogen fluoride has a wide range of industrial applications. It is used in the fluorination of polymers to produce fluorocarbons, in petroleum refining, glass manufacturing, aluminum production, titanium pickling, quartz purification, and metal finishing. It is also employed in the synthesis of uranium hexafluoride (UF₆), which is essential for the separation of uranium isotopes. In consumer products, HF can be found in formulations for rust removal, brass cleaning, and glass etching, although its use in such products is discouraged due to its corrosive and toxic nature. HF is typically marketed in three common forms: anhydrous HF, aqueous 70% HF, and aqueous 49% HF. Industrially, HF is produced by reacting calcium fluoride (fluorspar) with sulfuric acid. The vapors generated from this reaction contain a mixture of hydrogen fluoride, sulfuric acid, and minor byproducts. When hydrogen fluoride comes into contact with moisture, including tissue, it rapidly converts to hydrofluoric acid. This acid is highly corrosive and toxic, posing significant health risks upon exposure.
